general.temas: The post-Brexit relationship between the United Kingdom and the EU features prominently in The Guardian, Daily Mail and Daily Mirror, with differing assessments of the agreements. Crime and court proceedings, entertainment news and the war involving Russia, Ukraine and Poland also recur. The Guardian and Daily Mail report the arrest of teacher Sally-Anne Bowen. Only The Guardian highlights the international resurgence of measles.
general.motivo_crispacion: The agreements with the EU are generating political conflict: Daily Mail presents them as a concession, while Daily Mirror reports criticism from Nigel Farage. The war adds to international tensions, with attacks attributed to Russia and British reactions. Also prominent are an alleged antisemitic incident under police investigation and the conviction of a far-right activist for damaging a boat carrying asylum seekers. Cultural, entertainment and weather stories partly offset this atmosphere.

The Guardian.resumen:
- Burnham agrees trade and youth mobility measures with the EU, although student fees could complicate them.
- Measles is spreading again in several countries; a survivor recounts a drug-facilitated rape.
- Farage says he sees no one else more capable of leading Reform UK; a far-right activist is convicted of damaging a boat carrying asylum seekers.
- The Nasdaq loses its 2026 gains amid a sell-off of artificial intelligence stocks.
- The front page features an interview with Peter Gabriel, a review of the series about Melania Trump and an article about Lewis Hamilton’s activism.
The Guardian.motivo_populismo: Some headlines use satire and hyperbole, such as Farage’s “bitter heart” and the review that says it lost all sense of time and space, while others maintain a factual tone.
The Guardian.sesgo: The selection gives space to social issues and victims, and presents closer ties with the EU in favourable terms in a satirical column. It also includes critical takes on Farage and the series about Melania Trump, primarily in opinion and review pieces.

The Telegraph.resumen:
- Esther Rantzen, BBC presenter and founder of Childline, dies aged 86.
- Police are investigating the death of a girl in Surrey, a fatal stabbing in Northampton and a vehicle fire outside a London synagogue.
- Ministers will announce measures to tighten rules on foreign political donations and shell companies.
- Other incidents include an arrest on suspicion of rape, a hit-and-run and a cyberattack on a nursery chain.
- The front page also covers possible risks for 2026, a controversy over a British flag, and entertainment and promotional content for the newspaper.
The Telegraph.motivo_populismo: Factual headlines predominate, but phrases such as “the woke left has started to devour itself”, the “you’ll never guess what happened” formula and warnings of a possible pandemic worse than COVID add confrontation and sensationalism.
The Telegraph.sesgo: The selection highlights violent incidents, security and threats. The column on the flag takes a critical approach to the left and what it calls “woke”.

The Independent.resumen:
- An examination revealed that the hat swallowed by Fiona the hippopotamus was in her small intestine.
- A court approved a settlement of up to $7.25 billion with Bayer over claims related to the weedkiller Roundup.
- The front page carries criticism of an appearance by Trump, updates on the 2028 Democratic race and the bribery conviction of a former Democratic mayor.
- Police officers who lied about the search for missing women after a fatal crash in Cardiff were dismissed.
- Entertainment stories about “I’m A Celebrity”, a comedy review, a concert and recommendations for visiting Rhodes also feature prominently.
The Independent.motivo_populismo: Some headlines use dramatic language and put-downs, such as “drama erupts” and “comedic black hole”, but there are hardly any appeals to the people or portrayals of conflict between the people and elites.
The Independent.sesgo: The selection gives considerable weight to entertainment and personal conflicts. In politics, it features a critical portrayal of Trump, although this front page alone does not establish an overall party-political leaning.

Daily Mail.resumen:
- A mother loses her 18-year-old daughter, ten years after her son died in a road accident.
- The front page highlights stories about Meghan, Coleen Rooney and Geri Halliwell, as well as videos and files about UFOs.
- Burnham advocates a closer relationship with the EU; missile strikes in Poland following remarks by Trump are also reported.
- Incidents include children abandoned at a nursery, the stabbing of a councillor and a case of abuse of a pupil.
- British public borrowing reached £17 billion in October.
Daily Mail.motivo_populismo: Alarmist and sensationalist language abounds, such as “house of horrors” and “twisted scheme”, along with confrontational phrasing such as “surrender summit” and “brutal ambush”, although there are hardly any explicit appeals to the people against the elites.
Daily Mail.sesgo: The selection prioritises dramatic incidents, celebrities and eye-catching stories. In politics, the wording presents closer ties with the EU and the Labour government’s spending critically.

Daily Mirror.resumen:
- Andy Burnham’s government reaches agreements with the EU and proposes further changes to the post-Brexit relationship.
- Russia launches attacks on Ukraine; the United Kingdom condemns another attack on Poland and Denmark reports an alleged Russian plot against a rapper.
- Disputes between contestants on “I’m A Celebrity” and the Royal Variety charity performance feature on the front page.
- Chelsea is fined over anti-Catholic and anti-Irish chanting; the king is reported to be set to pay the mansion tax.
- A man is on trial for the alleged murder of a female friend, whose body he is said to have kept in a freezer.
Daily Mirror.motivo_populismo: Derogatory expressions such as “rubbish deal” about Brexit and “reckless attack” stand out, alongside sensationalist details about television disputes and an alleged murder.
Daily Mirror.sesgo: The front page presents Burnham’s efforts to move closer to the EU favourably and criticises Boris Johnson’s Brexit deal. It also adopts a markedly critical tone towards Putin and Trump’s attitude to him.

opiniones.comunista:
I see the agreements with the European Union as an opportunity to facilitate trade and youth mobility, but I do not confuse open markets with emancipation. If the benefits remain in the hands of big business while workers bear the uncertainty, we will have changed the rules without changing the distribution of power. I want cooperation between peoples, workers’ rights and democratic control of the economy.

The resurgence of measles is a reminder of what is at stake when health is treated as a cost rather than a right. In the face of volatile investment in artificial intelligence and the debate over public debt, I advocate strong public services and collective ownership of strategic sectors. The wealth we produce should be used to care, prevent illness and guarantee a dignified life, not primarily to boost returns for big capital.
opiniones.anarquista:
I am pleased that the agreements between the United Kingdom and the EU make it easier for young people to move between them. Being able to cross borders to study and work expands freedom; I wish it did not depend on negotiations between governments that make decisions on behalf of those who have little voice in them. I do not believe that changing the party or the leader is enough to stop our lives being subordinated to those decisions.

The resurgence of measles, with children paying the price, is a reminder that freedom also requires shared care. I support accessible healthcare, clear information and communities able to organise alongside professionals, without reducing people to mere recipients of orders.

Instead of state and economic hierarchies, I prefer mutual aid networks and self-managed spaces: institutions that we can build, control and transform from the bottom up.
opiniones.liberal:
I welcome the agreements to facilitate trade with the European Union and youth mobility. Being able to sell, work and study with fewer barriers expands individual opportunities. But my support is not a blank cheque: I want to know the terms and make sure they do not replace one set of obstacles with another.

I am also concerned that public borrowing reached £17 billion in October despite increased tax revenues. I do not believe that always asking taxpayers for more money is a sustainable strategy. I prefer low taxes, spending guided by clear priorities and a limited state that protects rights without trying to direct every economic decision. The fall in the Nasdaq is also a reminder that investing involves risks: those seeking profits must also bear the losses, without expecting taxpayers to cover them.
opiniones.extrema_derecha:
I am not opposed to trading with Europe, but I reject the idea that every concession to Brussels should be presented as inevitable progress. The agreements on food, emissions and youth mobility deserve public scrutiny: how much power does the United Kingdom retain to set its own rules and control who enters and stays here? Cooperation must not become a back door for undoing our regained sovereignty.

I also welcome plans to tighten the rules on foreign political donations. A national democracy cannot allow shell companies to buy influence. But security requires more than announcements: the attack on a synagogue that is under investigation is a reminder of the duty to protect our communities and pursue hatred with the full force of the law. And with borrowing still high, no government should ask for trust without explaining how it will pay for its decisions.
opiniones.centro:
I see the agreements with the European Union as an opportunity to replace years of confrontation with practical cooperation. Making it easier to trade food and drink and for young people to move between countries can benefit businesses and families alike. I do not regard negotiation as surrender: responsible sovereignty also means reaching useful compromises. But the possible obstacle of university fees shows that the details matter as much as the announcements.

I am also concerned that the United States, Mexico and Bolivia have lost their measles-free status. Protecting children requires reliable health institutions and vaccination campaigns that inspire confidence.

With public borrowing high in the United Kingdom, I do not promise cost-free solutions. I prefer gradual reforms, well-assessed public investment and a market economy that generates the resources to sustain strong social protection.
